prime.problem: Every graph algorithm in this course repeats one step millions of times: "give me the neighbours of u". If the storage makes that step read every edge, or every vertex, BFS and Dijkstra quietly become O(V·E) or O(V²) and the complexity you were promised is gone.
prime.fits: First card of the graph part. It builds on hash maps from course 1 (a dict of dicts is the adjacency list) and sets up the running example graph that the next eleven cards reuse.
expect: adjacency list as a dict of dicts (V + E entries)
implicit graphs: a grid computes its own neighbours
prime.goal: Choose a representation by the query your algorithm repeats, and state what that query costs in each one.

attend: Which question does each representation answer in O(1), and which does it answer slowly?
Why does the matrix cost 25 cells for 7 edges here, and what does that ratio become at V = 10⁴, E = 5 × 10⁴?
Why is a whole BFS O(V + E) with a list but O(V²) with a matrix, when the traversal code is the same?
For the island problems, why store no edges at all, and what does the choice k = 4 or k = 8 change?

must: BFS/DFS/Dijkstra repeat "neighbours of u" → an adjacency list reads only deg(u) entries → the whole walk costs O(V + E) → a matrix reads a full row of V cells each time → O(V²)

A matrix reserves a cell for every possible pair → space V² regardless of edges → 10⁸ cells for a sparse 10⁴-vertex graph vs 60,000 list entries → only worth it when the graph is dense or the algorithm (Floyd–Warshall) indexes pairs
A grid's neighbours follow from (i, j) → compute them on demand (implicit graph) → no storage, and the connectivity rule k = 4 or 8 decides how many islands exist (2 vs 1 on the card's grid)
elevated: Undirected edges are stored twice (u→v and v→u) → 2E list entries and a symmetric matrix → forgetting the second direction silently disconnects the graph
reference: the source's Graph(V, E) API and its method list
CSR (compressed sparse row) as scipy's packed form

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the course's 5-node graph three ways (edge list, matrix, dict of dicts) and label each with its space and its cost for "neighbours of C". Then say in two sentences which one you default to and when you would switch.
checklist: edge list: O(E) space, neighbours cost O(E)
matrix: O(V²) space (25 cells), edge test O(1), neighbours O(V)
dict of dicts: O(V + E) space (12 entries), edge test O(1) average, neighbours O(deg)
default to the list; a matrix for dense graphs or all-pairs tables; an edge list for sweep-every-edge algorithms (Kruskal, Bellman–Ford)

retrieve.q: Explain why the choice of representation changes an algorithm's complexity even when the algorithm's code is identical.
answer: the algorithm's inner loop is "for each neighbour of u"
its cost per vertex is deg(u) with a list, V with a matrix, E with an edge list
summed over all vertices: V + E, V², V·E

retrieve.q: Trace get_neighbors(grid, 1, 1, color=1, k=8) on the card's grid: which offsets are tried, which pass the bounds check, and which pass the colour check?
answer: all 8 offsets are in bounds for (1, 1) on a 4 × 4 grid
the colour check keeps cells equal to 1: (0, 1), (0, 0), (2, 2)
k = 4 would keep only (0, 1), which is why the island count is 2 with k = 4 and 1 with k = 8

retrieve.q: Floyd–Warshall on 100 cities, Kruskal on 10⁵ edges, BFS on a social graph with 10⁶ users: pick a representation for each and name the cost it saves.
answer: Floyd–Warshall: a matrix; it indexes dist[i][j] for every pair anyway, and 10⁴ cells is small
Kruskal: an edge list; it sorts and sweeps every edge once and never asks for neighbours
BFS: an adjacency list; the graph is sparse, so a matrix would need 10¹² cells

compare.q: The adjacency list here is a dict of dicts. What does hashing buy for the edge test "B" in E["C"] compared with a list of lists, and when would the list of lists be the better choice?
answer: dict: O(1) average edge test via hashing
list of lists: edge test is O(deg u), but less memory and faster iteration
choose the list of lists when you only ever iterate neighbours (BFS, DFS) and vertices are small integers

compare.q: This card's grid is an implicit graph. What does the flood-fill card gain by never building an adjacency list, and what would building one cost on a 1000 × 1000 grid?
answer: flood fill just needs neighbours on demand, computed from (i, j) in O(1)
building a list would store about 4 entries per cell, roughly 4 × 10⁶ entries, before any search starts
implicit keeps memory at the grid plus the stack

predict.q: You make the course's graph undirected. Predict the number of adjacency-list entries and the number of filled matrix cells, and whether the matrix is now symmetric.
predict.answer: Each of the 7 edges is stored in both directions: 14 list entries (plus the 5 keys) and 14 filled cells out of 25, and the matrix becomes symmetric about its diagonal. The empty share drops from 72% to 44%, but the matrix still pays 25 cells regardless.

apply.task: Extend to_adj to also build a reverse adjacency (predecessors) in the same pass, and use it on the course's graph to list who points into D and into E. Then say which algorithm in this course needs the reverse direction.
apply.done: Your predecessors are D: {B, C} and E: {C, D} (and B: {A, C}, C: {A}), built in one O(E) pass; you can name bidirectional BFS (the backward search) as a user.
apply.hint: One extra line inside the loop: R[v][u] = w.

reflect: Which cost surprised you: the matrix's empty cells, or the edge list's O(V·E) BFS?
Could you explain why an implicit grid is still a graph, without drawing it?
Which prediction did you get wrong in the undirected version?
Which link is fuzzy: representation → neighbour cost, or neighbour cost → total BFS cost?
Which later card will you watch for the representation it assumes?
